Antonio Pirri - Saint Francis Recieving the Stigmata (1525-30)

There's a lot going on in this painting. I like the way Pirri just painted in whatever he felt like painting in, without any regard to how likely it was to exist in this scene. Of course his perspective is wonky, but that just lends the painting a greater charm.

Who's the fat little old guy in white in the cave. He looks as though he's talking to somebody behind that rock, but the other person, or spirit, is hidden. He must be a saint because he's got a halo around his head.

Christ on a cross floating in the sky is downright strange looking. He looks about six inches tall, for one thing. He also looks like some kind of weird fairy with wings and antlers. He's shooting down rays to pierce the body of St. Francis -- one from each foot, one from each hand, and one from the side. But strangely, no ray from the head. Light is pouring out of the holes these five divine rays have drilled into the body of the saint.

The landscape is like something from Hieronymous Bosch. Impossible craigs of jagged rock, little rectangular mats of grass, and little animals everywhere, which of course St. Francis was known for having around him. The owl in the tree over his head is a curious choice, given the owl's evil associations, but there's a rabbit behind him, a pair of ducks, a stork, a swan, a couple of bucks.

Then in the distance you've got tiny human figures with tiny horses, both up on the hills to the right and left, and in the background in the middle. Churches appear on these hills beside the people, so I guess the people must be church goers.

One of the most fascinating aspects of the painting in the center background, which just keeps getting stranger and stranger the closer you get to the distant horizon. First there are people riding horses in a field -- looks like some kind of recreational activity, or maybe preparations for a hunt. Behind them you have what looks like a cathedral, then a body of water, then these fantastic towers on the horizon that don't like like any conventional earthly architecture of the 16th century. It's like the artist painted this work on LSD.
